claim: DNa01 and DNa02 project to all three leg neuromeres in the ventral nerve cord.
source: DNa01 and DNa02 project to all three leg neuromeres in the ventral nerve cord (Figure 1A), where they form selective connections onto leg-control networks (Braun et al., 2024; Cheong et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Braun et al., 2024 and Cheong et al., 2023, and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 form selective connections onto leg-control networks.
source: DNa01 and DNa02 project to all three leg neuromeres in the ventral nerve cord (Figure 1A), where they form selective connections onto leg-control networks (Braun et al., 2024; Cheong et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Braun et al., 2024 and Cheong et al., 2023.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 are anatomically similar to cricket neurons that are active during turning.
source: These DNs are anatomically similar to cricket neurons that are active during turning (Brodfuehrer and Hoy, 1990; Staudacher and Schildberger, 1998; Zorović and Hedwig, 2011), and a calcium imaging study reported that DNa01 is asymmetrically active in the ventral nerve cord when flies are turning (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brodfuehrer and Hoy, 1990; Staudacher and Schildberger, 1998; Zorović and Hedwig, 2011.

claim: DNa01 is asymmetrically active in the ventral nerve cord when flies are turning.
source: These DNs are anatomically similar to cricket neurons that are active during turning (Brodfuehrer and Hoy, 1990; Staudacher and Schildberger, 1998; Zorović and Hedwig, 2011), and a calcium imaging study reported that DNa01 is asymmetrically active in the ventral nerve cord when flies are turning (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: Bilateral activation of DNa01 or DNa02 drives a global increase in walking.
source: On the other hand, an optogenetic perturbation study reported that bilateral activation of DNa01 or DNa02 drives a global increase in walking (Cande et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cande et al., 2018.

claim: DNa02 makes more direct synaptic connections onto motor neurons compared to DNa01.
source: In analyzing the ventral nerve cord connectome (Cheong et al., 2023), we noticed that DNa02 makes more direct synaptic connections onto motor neurons, as compared to DNa01 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheong et al., 2023 and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Very few of the postsynaptic cells targeted by DNa01 and DNa02 are shared in common.
source: Moreover, very few of the postsynaptic cells targeted by these two DN types are shared in common (Cheong et al., 2023; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheong et al., 2023 and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Both DNa01 and DNa02 are depolarized just before the fly steers in the ipsilateral direction.
source: Both cells are depolarized just before the fly steers in the ipsilateral direction (asterisks).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D with asterisks marking the events.

claim: Both DNa01 and DNa02 are hyperpolarized when the fly briefly stops moving.
source: Both cells are hyperpolarized when the fly briefly stops moving (arrowhead).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D with an arrowhead marking the event.

claim: DNa02 has more transient fluctuations compared to DNa01.
source: Notably, DNa02 had more transient fluctuations, as compared to DNa01 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spike rate fluctuations in DNa02 typically preceded the spike rate fluctuations in DNa01.
source: Moreover, spike rate fluctuations in DNa02 typically preceded the spike rate fluctuations in DNa01 (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 firing rate increases are typically followed by relatively large changes in rotational and sideways velocity.
source: These filters showed that DNa01 and DNa02 firing rate increases were typically followed by relatively large changes in rotational and sideways velocity (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 firing rate increases were not consistently followed by large changes in forward velocity.
source: DNa01 and DNa02 firing rate increases were not consistently followed by large changes in forward velocity (Figure 2C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Steering filters were larger for DNa02 than for DNa01.
source: First, steering filters (i.e. rotational and sideways velocity filters) were larger for DNa02 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: DNa02 operates with higher gain than DNa01.
source: This means that an impulse change in firing rate predicts a larger change in steering for this neuron. In other words, this result suggests that DNa02 operates with higher gain.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that steering filters are larger for DNa02.

claim: DNa02 steering filters were biphasic, whereas DNa01 steering filters were monophasic.
source: Moreover, we found that DNa02 steering filters were biphasic, whereas DNa01 steering filters were monophasic (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: A biphasic filter converts a sustained input into a transient output, while a monophasic filter converts a sustained input into a sustained output.
source: A biphasic filter converts a sustained input into a transient output, while a monophasic filter converts a sustained input into a sustained output.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of signal processing and filter characteristics.

claim: DNa02 produces more transient changes in steering compared to DNa01.
source: This result suggests that DNa02 produces more transient changes in steering, as compared to DNa01.
evidence: Inferred from the biphasic nature of DNa02 filters versus monophasic nature of DNa01 filters.

claim: DNa02 filters produced a better prediction of the fly's subsequent steering compared to DNa01 filters.
source: Finally, we found that steering filters for DNa02 were more accurately predictive of behavior – i.e., when we convolved each filter with the cell's spike train, the DNa02 filters produced a better prediction of the fly's subsequent steering, as compared to the DNa01 filters (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: DNa02 fires more transiently than DNa01.
source: To recap, DNa02 fires more transiently than DNa01, and it is also recruited before DNa01 (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: DNa02 is recruited before DNa01.
source: To recap, DNa02 fires more transiently than DNa01, and it is also recruited before DNa01 (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The behavioral impulse response is more transient for DNa02 than for DNa01.
source: But even if we normalize for the firing rate dynamics of each cell type, the behavioral impulse response is also more transient for DNa02 than for DNa01 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: DNa02 is associated with more transient steering events compared to DNa01.
source: In other words, DNa02 impulses arrive in relatively transient packets and each DNa02 impulse predicts a relatively transient change in behavior; for both these reasons, DNa02 is associated with more transient steering events, as compared to DNa01.
evidence: Inferred from the transient firing patterns and transient behavioral impulse responses of DNa02.

claim: Rotational velocity was a relatively steep function of DNa02 activity.
source: We observed that rotational velocity was a relatively steep function of DNa02 activity, but a comparatively shallower function of DNa01 activity (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F–H.

claim: Rotational velocity was a comparatively shallower function of DNa01 activity.
source: We observed that rotational velocity was a relatively steep function of DNa02 activity, but a comparatively shallower function of DNa01 activity (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F–H.

claim: There is a higher-gain relationship between DNa02 activity and steering.
source: This analysis supports the conclusion that there is a higher-gain relationship between DNa02 activity and steering.
evidence: Inferred from the steeper relationship between DNa02 activity and rotational velocity.

claim: Rotational velocity was consistently related to the difference in right-left DNa02 firing rates.
source: We found that rotational velocity was consistently related to the difference in right-left firing rates (Figure 3B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The relationship between rotational velocity and right-left DNa02 firing rate difference was essentially linear through its entire dynamic range.
source: This relationship was essentially linear through its entire dynamic range, and was consistent across paired recordings (Figure 3C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The relationship between rotational velocity and right-left DNa02 firing rate difference was consistent during backward walking as well as forward walking.
source: It was also consistent during backward walking, as well as forward walking (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar results were obtained in dual recordings from DNa01 neurons.
source: We obtained similar results in dual recordings from DNa01 neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: By adding the predictions from simultaneously recorded right-left DNa02 pairs, we could accurately predict turns in both directions.
source: By adding the predictions from simultaneously recorded right-left pairs, we found that we could accurately predict turns in both directions (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Steering is consistently predicted by right-left differences in DNa02 firing rate.
source: To summarize, these dual recordings demonstrate that steering is consistently predicted by right-left differences in DNa02 firing rate.
evidence: Summarizes findings from dual recordings.

claim: Turning could be driven by either ipsilateral excitation or contralateral inhibition.
source: This means that, in principle, turning could be driven by either ipsilateral excitation or contralateral inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that steering is predicted by right-left differences in DNa02 firing rate.

claim: The neural networks in the brain presynaptic to DNa02 are organized to recruit both ipsilateral excitation and contralateral inhibition.
source: As we will see, the neural networks in the brain presynaptic to these DNs are organized so as to recruit both ipsilateral excitation and contralateral inhibition.
evidence: Refers to subsequent connectome analysis findings.

claim: Head direction neurons (EPG neurons) can influence steering.
source: Head direction neurons (EPG neurons) (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015) can influence steering (Giraldo et al., 2018; Green et al., 2019) via central complex neurons that compare head direction signals with internal goal signals (Beetz et al., 2022; Martin et al., 2015; Mussells Pires et al., 2024; Shiozaki et al., 2020; Westeinde et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Giraldo et al., 2018; Green et al., 2019; Beetz et al., 2022; Martin et al., 2015; Mussells Pires et al., 2024; Shiozaki et al., 2020; Westeinde et al., 2024.

claim: The central complex contains no DNs.
source: The central complex itself contains no DNs (Hulse et al., 2021; Namiki et al., 2018), but there are strong anatomical pathways from the central complex to DNa02 (Hulse et al., 2021; Mussells Pires et al., 2024; Rayshubskiy et al., 2020; Westeinde et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hulse et al., 2021; Namiki et al., 2018.

claim: There are strong anatomical pathways from the central complex to DNa02.
source: The central complex itself contains no DNs (Hulse et al., 2021; Namiki et al., 2018), but there are strong anatomical pathways from the central complex to DNa02 (Hulse et al., 2021; Mussells Pires et al., 2024; Rayshubskiy et al., 2020; Westeinde et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hulse et al., 2021; Mussells Pires et al., 2024; Rayshubskiy et al., 2020; Westeinde et al., 2024.

claim: DNa02 participates in steering toward internal goals.
source: This motivated our hypothesis that DNa02 participates in steering toward internal goals.
evidence: Hypothesis based on anatomical connectivity between central complex and DNa02.

claim: PEN1 neurons relay information about the fly's angular velocity to EPG neurons.
source: PEN1 neurons relay information about the fly's angular velocity to EPG neurons, and so micro-stimulating PEN1 neurons causes the head direction system to register a fictive behavioral turn.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PEN1 neuron function.

claim: Micro-stimulating PEN1 neurons causes the head direction system to register a fictive behavioral turn.
source: PEN1 neurons relay information about the fly's angular velocity to EPG neurons, and so micro-stimulating PEN1 neurons causes the head direction system to register a fictive behavioral turn.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PEN1 neuron function and experimental design.

claim: There is a single bump of activity in the EPG ensemble whose angular velocity generally correlates with the fly's angular velocity.
source: As expected from previous work, we found that there is a single bump of activity in the EPG ensemble whose angular velocity generally correlates with the fly's angular velocity (Green et al., 2017; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Turner-Evans et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Green et al., 2017; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Turner-Evans et al., 2017.

claim: The position of the EPG bump constitutes a working memory of the fly's heading direction.
source: The position of the EPG bump constitutes a working memory of the fly's heading direction.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of EPG neuron function.

claim: Briefly micro-stimulating PEN1 neurons causes the EPG bump to 'jump' to a new location.
source: Again, consistent with previous work, we found that briefly micro-stimulating PEN1 neurons causes this bump to 'jump' to a new location (Green et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Green et al., 2019 and experimental data.

claim: Bump jumps rarely follow ATP injection when the Gal4 transgene is omitted.
source: As a negative control, we confirmed that bump jumps rarely follow ATP injection when the Gal4 transgene is omitted (Figure 4B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B as a negative control.

claim: The fly typically executes a compensatory behavioral turn shortly after the EPG bump jump.
source: Accordingly, we find that the fly typically executes a compensatory behavioral turn shortly after the EPG bump jump, as reported previously (Green et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Green et al., 2019 and experimental data.

claim: The compensatory turn brought the EPG bump back to its initial location in 40% of trials.
source: This compensatory turn brought the EPG bump back to its initial location in 40% of trials, thereby re-orienting the fly toward its inferred internal goal.
evidence: Based on experimental data.

claim: In trials where the ATP injection caused the bump to jump clockwise, the behavioral turn was typically rightward.
source: Notably, in trials where the ATP injection caused the bump to jump clockwise, the behavioral turn was typically rightward, which causes the bump to flow counter-clockwise (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: In trials where the ATP injection caused the bump to jump counter-clockwise, the average behavioral turn was leftward.
source: Conversely, on trials where the injection caused the bump to jump counter-clockwise, the average behavioral turn was leftward, which causes the bump to flow clockwise (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The compensatory turn was in the correct direction to return the bump to its original location via the shortest path.
source: Thus, the compensatory turn was in the correct direction to return the bump to its original location via the shortest path.
evidence: Inferred from the directional relationship between bump jumps and behavioral turns.

claim: The mechanism that triggers the compensatory turn is sensitive to the direction of the error (positive or negative).
source: This implies that the mechanism that triggers the compensatory turn is sensitive to the direction of the error (positive or negative).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that compensatory turns are in the correct direction to return the bump via the shortest path.

claim: DNa02 cells often fired a burst of spikes just before the fly performed its compensatory behavioral turn to bring the EPG bump back to its initial location.
source: Notably, we found that DNa02 cells often fired a burst of spikes just before the fly performed its compensatory behavioral turn to bring the EPG bump back to its initial location (Figure 4E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The bump jump was typically followed by increased DNa02 firing on the left, and then a leftward steering maneuver, and then a clockwise return of the bump.
source: In these trials, we found that the bump jump was typically followed by increased DNa02 firing on the left, and then a leftward steering maneuver, and then a clockwise return of the bump (Figure 4F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4F.

claim: DNa02 could predict much of the trial-to-trial variability in the magnitude of compensatory behavioral turns.
source: Moreover, we found that DNa02 could predict much of the trial-to-trial variability in the magnitude of compensatory behavioral turns (Figure 4G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4G.

claim: In trials where the bump returned counter-clockwise, the fly's behavioral turn was typically rightward rather than leftward.
source: In these trials, the fly's behavioral turn was typically rightward rather than leftward (Figure 4E and H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4E and H.

claim: There was no DNa02 firing rate increase on the left side in trials where the bump returned counter-clockwise.
source: Accordingly, we found no DNa02 firing rate increase on the left side (Figure 4H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4H.

claim: DNa02 is not activated bilaterally and thus nonspecifically.
source: This shows that DNa02 is not activated bilaterally and thus nonspecifically.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DNa02 is only activated on the side predicting the direction of the behavioral turn.

claim: DNa02 is recruited specifically on the side that predicts the direction of the behavioral turn.
source: Rather, DNa02 is recruited specifically on the side that predicts the direction of the behavioral turn.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing side-specific DNa02 activation.

claim: DNa02 activity can predict the magnitude and direction of steering maneuvers guided by the head direction system.
source: In summary, our results show that DNa02 activity can predict the magnitude and direction of steering maneuvers guided by the head direction system.
evidence: Summarizes findings from head direction system experiments.

claim: The pathways from head direction system to DNa02 are functionally strong.
source: This finding argues that the pathways from head direction system to DNa02 are functionally strong, and they are recruited at the appropriate time to mediate steering commands issuing from the central complex.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DNa02 activity predicts steering maneuvers guided by the head direction system.

claim: Pathways from head direction system to DNa02 are recruited at the appropriate time to mediate steering commands issuing from the central complex.
source: This finding argues that the pathways from head direction system to DNa02 are functionally strong, and they are recruited at the appropriate time to mediate steering commands issuing from the central complex.
evidence: Inferred from the timing of DNa02 activation relative to steering maneuvers.

claim: Flies often turn toward a lateralized odor.
source: This fictive odor stimulus produced steering toward the stimulated antenna (Figure 5A), consistent with previous studies showing that flies often turn toward a lateralized odor (Borst and Heisenberg, 1982; Gaudry et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Borst and Heisenberg, 1982; Gaudry et al., 2013, and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Lateralized fictive odor stimuli produced asymmetric responses in DNa02, with higher firing rates on the ipsilateral side.
source: We found that these lateralized stimuli also produced asymmetric responses in DNa02, with higher firing rates on the ipsilateral side (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Lateralized fictive odor stimuli often produced hyperpolarization and a suppression of spiking in the contralateral DN.
source: Interestingly, these stimuli often produced hyperpolarization and a suppression of spiking in the contralateral DN, suggesting that ipsilateral excitation is accompanied by contralateral inhibition.
evidence: Based on experimental data.

claim: Ipsilateral excitation is accompanied by contralateral inhibition in response to lateralized fictive odor stimuli.
source: Interestingly, these stimuli often produced hyperpolarization and a suppression of spiking in the contralateral DN, suggesting that ipsilateral excitation is accompanied by contralateral inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of contralateral hyperpolarization during ipsilateral excitation.

claim: There was no neural or behavioral response when the LexA transgene was omitted.
source: We also confirmed there was no neural or behavioral response when the LexA transgene was omitted (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), as expected.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 as a negative control.

claim: Fictive heat drives behavioral turning away from the stimulus.
source: These fictive warm stimuli drove flies to steer away from the stimulated antenna (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fictive heat stimuli produced responses in DNa02, with higher firing rates on the side contralateral to the stimulus.
source: These stimuli again produced responses in DNa02, but now with higher firing rates on the side contralateral to the stimulus (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DNa02 activity was higher on the side ipsilateral to the attractive stimulus, but contralateral to the aversive stimulus.
source: Thus, DNa02 activity was higher on the side ipsilateral to the attractive stimulus, but contralateral to the aversive stimulus.
evidence: Based on experimental data from fictive odor and fictive heat experiments.

claim: DNa02 encoded the laterality of the stimulus-evoked action, not the laterality of the stimulus itself.
source: In other words, DNa02 encoded the laterality of the stimulus-evoked action, not the laterality of the stimulus itself.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DNa02 activity depends on the direction of the behavioral response, not the side of the stimulus.

claim: DNa02 was activated about 150ms before the stimulus-evoked turn.
source: On average, DNa02 was activated about 150ms before the stimulus-evoked turn (Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DNa02 could predict much of the trial-to-trial variability in the magnitude of stimulus-evoked turns.
source: Moreover, DNa02 could predict much of the trial-to-trial variability in the magnitude of stimulus-evoked turns (Figure 5D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5D.

claim: DNa02 participates in reorienting the body in response to a lateralized stimulus.
source: Together, these findings suggest that DNa02 participates in reorienting the body in response to a lateralized stimulus.
evidence: Inferred from the timing and predictive power of DNa02 activity relative to stimulus-evoked turns.

claim: Similar results were obtained for DNa01 neurons.
source: We obtained similar results for DNa01 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), supporting the idea that DNa01 and DNa02 often function together.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: DNa02 hyperpolarized whenever the fly stopped walking.
source: Although DNa02 hyperpolarized whenever the fly stopped walking (Figure 6A and B), it continued responding to lateralized odors even when the fly was stopped.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: DNa02 continued responding to lateralized odors even when the fly was stopped.
source: Although DNa02 hyperpolarized whenever the fly stopped walking (Figure 6A and B), it continued responding to lateralized odors even when the fly was stopped.
evidence: Based on experimental data.

claim: During immobility, the stimulus-evoked change in DNa02 firing rate was similar to what was observed during walking.
source: Indeed, during immobility, the stimulus-evoked change in DNa02 firing rate was similar to what we observed during walking (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: DNa02 contains information about latent steering drives, even in a quiescent behavioral state where these drives produce no measurable motor consequences.
source: This observation suggests that DNa02 contains information about latent steering drives, even in a quiescent behavioral state where these drives produce no measurable motor consequences.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DNa02 responds to stimuli during immobility.

claim: DNa02 integrates several different types of steering signals.
source: Our results thus far indicate that DNa02 integrates several different types of steering signals.
evidence: Summarizes findings from multiple experiments.

claim: DNa02 receives internal goal-directed steering signals from the central complex.
source: Specifically, it receives internal goal-directed steering signals from the central complex, as well as stimulus-directed steering signals from the olfactory system and the thermosensory system.
evidence: Based on experimental data from central complex stimulation and sensory stimulation experiments.

claim: DNa02 receives stimulus-directed steering signals from the olfactory system and the thermosensory system.
source: Specifically, it receives internal goal-directed steering signals from the central complex, as well as stimulus-directed steering signals from the olfactory system and the thermosensory system.
evidence: Based on experimental data from sensory stimulation experiments.

claim: DNa02 receives locomotor state signals that make the cell more depolarized when the fly is walking.
source: It also receives locomotor state signals that make the cell more depolarized when the fly is walking.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing DNa02 hyperpolarization during immobility.

claim: The inputs to DNa02 are largely non-overlapping with those of DNa01.
source: We found that the inputs to DNa02 are largely non-overlapping with those of DNa01 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7A based on connectome analysis.

claim: DNa02 can be recruited before DNa01, with a more transient pattern of activity.
source: This fits with our finding that DNa02 can be recruited before DNa01, with a more transient pattern of activity: the inputs to these cells are evidently somewhat independent.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological data and connectome analysis.

claim: Both DNa01 and DNa02 receive substantial input from central brain intrinsic neurons.
source: Both DNs receive substantial input from central brain intrinsic neurons; however, only DNa02 receives direct input from PFL3 cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 based on connectome analysis.

claim: Only DNa02 receives direct input from PFL3 cells.
source: Both DNs receive substantial input from central brain intrinsic neurons; however, only DNa02 receives direct input from PFL3 cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 based on connectome analysis.

claim: PFL3 cells compare head direction signals with internal goal signals.
source: PFL3 cells compare head direction signals with internal goal signals, and they produce directional steering commands if there is a mismatch between these angular values (Dan et al., 2024; Goulard et al., 2021; Hulse et al., 2021; Matheson et al., 2022; Mussells Pires et al., 2024; Rayshubskiy et al., 2020; Westeinde et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dan et al., 2024; Goulard et al., 2021; Hulse et al., 2021; Matheson et al., 2022; Mussells Pires et al., 2024; Rayshubskiy et al., 2020; Westeinde et al., 2024.

claim: PFL3 cells produce directional steering commands if there is a mismatch between head direction and internal goal signals.
source: PFL3 cells compare head direction signals with internal goal signals, and they produce directional steering commands if there is a mismatch between these angular values (Dan et al., 2024; Goulard et al., 2021; Hulse et al., 2021; Matheson et al., 2022; Mussells Pires et al., 2024; Rayshubskiy et al., 2020; Westeinde et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dan et al., 2024; Goulard et al., 2021; Hulse et al., 2021; Matheson et al., 2022; Mussells Pires et al., 2024; Rayshubskiy et al., 2020; Westeinde et al., 2024.

claim: PFL3 neurons are the likely origin of the turning signals seen in DNa02 when an error signal is chemogenetically injected into the head direction system.
source: PFL3 neurons are, therefore, the likely origin of the turning signals we see in DNa02 when we chemogenetically inject an error signal into the head direction system (Figure 4).
evidence: Inferred from the connectivity between PFL3 and DNa02, and the experimental results in Figure 4.

claim: PFL3 neurons send many strong indirect projections to DNa02.
source: Notably, however, we found that PFL3 neurons also send many strong indirect projections to DNa02.
evidence: Based on connectome analysis.

claim: PFL3 neurons project to DNa03 and LAL010, which make strong excitatory ipsilateral connections onto DNa02.
source: Specifically, PFL3 neurons project to two cells (DNa03 and LAL010) that make strong excitatory ipsilateral connections onto DNa02 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7C based on connectome analysis.

claim: Indirect connections from PFL3 to DNa02 should amplify the influence of central complex steering signals.
source: These indirect connections should amplify the influence of central complex steering signals.
evidence: Inferred from the connectivity pattern.

claim: PFL3 neurons project to several cell types that are positioned to inhibit the contralateral copies of DNa02, DNa03, and LAL010.
source: Moreover, PFL3 neurons also project to several cell types that are positioned to inhibit the contralateral copies of DNa02, DNa03, and LAL010 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7C based on connectome analysis.

claim: Contralateral suppression should increase the right-left difference in DNa02 activity, thereby increasing rotational velocity.
source: Contralateral suppression should increase the right-left difference in DNa02 activity, thereby increasing rotational velocity.
evidence: Inferred from the connectivity pattern and the relationship between right-left DNa02 activity difference and rotational velocity.

claim: Central complex projections are wired to have opposite effects on the two copies of DNa02.
source: In short, central complex projections are wired to have opposite effects on the two copies of DNa02.
evidence: Based on connectome analysis showing ipsilateral excitation and contralateral inhibition.

claim: This architecture suggests a 'see-saw' model of steering, where an increase in excitatory synaptic input in one DN is often accompanied by an increase in inhibitory synaptic input to the contralateral DN.
source: This architecture suggests a 'see-saw' model of steering, where an increase in excitatory synaptic input in one DN (and/or a disinhibition of that DN) is often accompanied by an increase in inhibitory synaptic input to the contralateral DN (Figure 7D).
evidence: Inferred from the connectivity pattern and illustrated in Figure 7D.

claim: The see-saw model is consistent with the observation that lateralized stimuli can excite one DN while inhibiting the contralateral DN.
source: This see-saw model is consistent with our observation that lateralized stimuli can excite one DN while inhibiting the contralateral DN.
evidence: Inferred from the consistency between the see-saw model and experimental observations.

claim: Some indirect connections onto DNa02 are bilaterally symmetric.
source: That said, some indirect connections onto DNa02 are actually bilaterally symmetric.
evidence: Based on connectome analysis.

claim: DNa03 and LAL010 both receive strong bilaterally symmetric projections from PFL2.
source: For example, DNa03 and LAL010 both receive strong bilaterally symmetric projections from another excitatory central complex output cell type, PFL2 (Figure 7E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7E based on connectome analysis.

claim: PFL2 neurons are recruited when the fly is oriented away from its internal goal.
source: PFL2 neurons are recruited when the fly is oriented away from its internal goal, and direct activation of PFL2 neurons increases the overall gain of steering commands, without specifying the direction of turning (Westeinde et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Westeinde et al., 2024.

claim: Direct activation of PFL2 neurons increases the overall gain of steering commands, without specifying the direction of turning.
source: PFL2 neurons are recruited when the fly is oriented away from its internal goal, and direct activation of PFL2 neurons increases the overall gain of steering commands, without specifying the direction of turning (Westeinde et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Westeinde et al., 2024.

claim: There are multiple pathways connecting olfactory and thermosensory peripheral cells to DNa02.
source: Outside the central complex, there are many pathways for stimulus-directed steering. For example, there are multiple pathways connecting olfactory and thermosensory peripheral cells to DNa02.
evidence: Based on connectome analysis.

claim: The shortest pathways connecting olfactory and thermosensory peripheral cells to DNa02 involve the mushroom body output neuron MBON32.
source: However, the shortest pathways involve the mushroom body output neuron MBON32 (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2020 and connectome analysis.

claim: MBON32 projections onto DNa02 are organized to produce see-saw steering: excitation onto one DN is generally accompanied by inhibition onto the other DN.
source: We found that MBON32 projections onto DNa02 are also organized to produce see-saw steering: excitation onto one DN is generally accompanied by inhibition onto the other DN (Figure 7F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7F based on connectome analysis.

claim: MBON32 projections could drive turning toward an appetitive stimulus, as well as turning away from an aversive stimulus.
source: Interestingly, MBON32 projections could drive turning toward an appetitive stimulus, as well as turning away from an aversive stimulus (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: Inferred from the connectivity pattern and illustrated in Figure 7G and H.

claim: There are generally two parallel pathways connecting any set of antennal lobe projection neurons to MBON32: a plastic excitatory pathway, and a fixed inhibitory pathway.
source: This idea derives from the fact that there are generally two parallel pathways connecting any set of antennal lobe projection neurons to MBON32: a plastic excitatory pathway, and a fixed inhibitory pathway.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mushroom body circuitry.

claim: Depression of the excitatory pathway (via Kenyon Cells) could unmask inhibition.
source: In principle, depression of the excitatory pathway (via Kenyon Cells, or KCs) could, therefore, unmask inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the parallel excitatory and inhibitory pathways.

claim: Depression of KC→MBON32 synapses should be driven by aversive stimuli, via the dopamine neuron PPL103.
source: Depression of KC→MBON32 synapses should be driven by aversive stimuli, via the dopamine neuron PPL103 (Cohn et al., 2015; Hige et al., 2015; Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Li et al., 2020; Perisse et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cohn et al., 2015; Hige et al., 2015; Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Li et al., 2020; Perisse et al., 2016.

claim: A stimulus with appetitive associations should produce excitation of MBON32, which would drive ipsiversive turning.
source: Therefore, a stimulus with appetitive associations, such as an appetitive odor, should produce excitation of MBON32, because the active KC→MBON synapses should be strong (not depressed); this would then drive ipsiversive turning.
evidence: Inferred from the plasticity of KC→MBON32 synapses and the connectivity pattern.

claim: A stimulus with aversive associations should produce inhibition of MBON32, which would drive contraversive turning.
source: Conversely, a stimulus with aversive associations, such as aversive heat, should produce inhibition of MBON32, because the active KC→MBON synapses should be weak (depressed), which would drive contraversive turning.
evidence: Inferred from the plasticity of KC→MBON32 synapses and the connectivity pattern.

claim: DNa02 receives abundant visual input.
source: Finally, connectome data shows that DNa02 receives abundant visual input.
evidence: Based on connectome analysis.

claim: Some visual input to DNa02 comes from a large set of visual projection neurons, which project directly from the optic lobe to DNa02.
source: Some of this input comes from a large set of visual projection neurons, which project directly from the optic lobe to DNa02 (Figure 7A) as well as DNa03 (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7A and supported by citation to Li et al., 2020.

claim: Another major source of visual input to DNa02 comes from projection neurons in the anterior optic tubercle, downstream from LC10 cells.
source: Another major source of input comes from projection neurons in the anterior optic tubercle, downstream from LC10 cells.
evidence: Based on connectome analysis.

claim: LC10 cells are small object motion detectors that mediate steering toward visual objects.
source: LC10 cells are small object motion detectors that mediate steering toward visual objects (Hindmarsh Sten et al., 2021; Ribeiro et al., 2018; Schretter et al., 2025).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hindmarsh Sten et al., 2021; Ribeiro et al., 2018; Schretter et al., 2025.

claim: Some visual signals arrive at DNa02 via MBON32, which receives visual input in addition to olfactory and thermo/hygrosensory input.
source: Some visual signals arrive via MBON32, which receives visual input in addition to olfactory and thermo/hygrosensory input (Figure 7F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7F based on connectome analysis.

claim: DNa02 is a site of integration for many steering control pathways.
source: In summary, DNa02 is a site of integration for many steering control pathways.
evidence: Summarizes findings from connectome analysis.

claim: Steering control pathways to DNa02 tend to be arranged for see-saw steering control: when one copy of DNa02 is excited, the other is inhibited.
source: These pathways tend to be arranged for see-saw steering control: when one copy of DNa02 is excited, the other is inhibited.
evidence: Based on connectome analysis.

claim: Many pathways to DNa02 involve parallel excitation and inhibition, which could provide a mechanism to specify steering direction based on excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance.
source: Many of these pathways involve parallel excitation and inhibition, which could provide a mechanism to specify steering direction based on excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance.
evidence: Inferred from the connectivity pattern.

claim: When one pathway to DNa02 is plastic, the change in E/I balance could provide a way to convert memory recall into a bidirectional behavioral readout.
source: When one pathway is plastic, the change in E/I balance could provide a way to convert memory recall into a bidirectional behavioral readout.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the connectivity pattern and plasticity.

claim: Unilateral optogenetic activation of DNa02 evoked a small average steering bias in the ipsilateral direction.
source: In the flies with unilateral expression, we found that light evoked a small average steering bias in the ipsilateral direction – i.e., the direction of the ReaChR +neuron (Figure 8B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The turning bias in flies with unilateral DNa02 expression was significantly larger than expected by chance.
source: We found that the mean of the data (with unilateral expression) was outside the 95% confidence interval of the simulation outcomes (Figure 8B and C). Thus, in flies with unilateral expression, the turning bias was significantly larger than we would expect by chance.
evidence: Shown in Figure 8B and C using statistical analysis.

claim: When DNa01 neurons were inhibited, sideways speed was significantly reduced.
source: When DNa01 neurons were inhibited, sideways speed was significantly reduced.
evidence: Based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Rotational speed was unchanged when either DNa01 or DNa02 neurons were inhibited.
source: Surprisingly, however, rotational speed was unchanged when either DNa01 or DNa02 neurons were inhibited.
evidence: Based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: In freely walking flies, body rotation can be achieved via many different leg maneuvers.
source: In freely walking flies, body rotation can be achieved via many different leg maneuvers (DeAngelis et al., 2019; Katsov et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to DeAngelis et al., 2019; Katsov et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2024.

claim: In some body-rotation events, the stance duration of the inner back leg is prolonged relative to the other legs.
source: For example, in some body-rotation events, the stance duration of the inner back leg is prolonged relative to the other legs – in essence, the fly pivots on its inner back leg – whereas this maneuver is absent in other body-rotation events (Figure 8F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Inhibiting DNa01 produced a significant defect in stance prolongation in the inner back leg.
source: We found that inhibiting DNa01 produced a significant defect in stance prolongation in the inner back leg – i.e., it reduced the fly's tendency to pivot on the inner back leg during a body rotation (Figure 8G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The same trend was observed when DNa02 was inhibited, although the trend fell short of statistical significance.
source: We observed the same trend when we inhibited DNa02, although here the trend fell short of statistical significance.
evidence: Based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Inhibiting DNa01 (and possibly DNa02) causes a defect in inner-back-leg-stance-prolongation, but this defect is compensated via other mechanisms to achieve a normal rotational movement of the body in freely moving flies.
source: These results suggest that inhibiting DNa01 (and possibly DNa02) causes a defect in inner-back-leg-stance-prolongation, but this defect is evidently compensated via other mechanisms to achieve a normal rotational movement of the body in freely moving flies.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that rotational speed is unchanged despite defects in specific leg maneuvers.

claim: Inhibiting either DNa01 or DNa02 altered the fly's normal leg movement rhythm, regardless of whether the fly was walking straight or turning.
source: We also noticed that inhibiting either DNa01 or DNa02 altered the fly's normal leg movement rhythm, regardless of whether the fly was walking straight or turning.
evidence: Based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Inhibiting either DNa01 or DNa02 increased step length and decreased step frequency.
source: Specifically, step length increased, while step frequency decreased (Figure 8H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Inhibiting DNa01 decreased the fly's forward velocity.
source: Inhibiting DNa01 also decreased the fly's forward velocity (Figure 8H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Both DNs can lengthen the stance phase of the ipsilateral back leg, which would promote ipsiversive turning.
source: That said, these results suggest that both DNs can lengthen the stance phase of the ipsilateral back leg, which would promote ipsiversive turning.
evidence: Inferred from the optogenetic inhibition results.

claim: Both DNs may decrease the step length in the ipsilateral legs, which would also promote ipsiversive turning.
source: These results are also compatible with a scenario where both DNs decrease the step length in the ipsilateral legs, which would also promote ipsiversive turning.
evidence: Inferred from the optogenetic inhibition results.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 are both recruited during turning bouts in walking flies.
source: In this study, we showed that DNa01 and DNa02 are both recruited during turning bouts in walking flies.
evidence: Summarizes findings from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 receive largely non-overlapping inputs in the brain.
source: However, connectome data shows these two DNs receive largely non-overlapping inputs in the brain, and they have largely non-overlapping outputs in the ventral nerve cord, suggesting that they represent parallel and largely independent pathways for steering control.
evidence: Based on connectome analysis.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 have largely non-overlapping outputs in the ventral nerve cord.
source: However, connectome data shows these two DNs receive largely non-overlapping inputs in the brain, and they have largely non-overlapping outputs in the ventral nerve cord, suggesting that they represent parallel and largely independent pathways for steering control.
evidence: Based on connectome analysis.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 represent parallel and largely independent pathways for steering control.
source: However, connectome data shows these two DNs receive largely non-overlapping inputs in the brain, and they have largely non-overlapping outputs in the ventral nerve cord, suggesting that they represent parallel and largely independent pathways for steering control.
evidence: Inferred from the non-overlapping inputs and outputs.

claim: DNa02 predicts large, rapid steering events, while DNa01 predicts smaller and slower steering events.
source: Importantly, our electrophysiological results in this study support this hypothesis: these two DN types have distinct functional profiles: DNa02 predicts large, rapid steering events, while DNa01 predicts smaller and slower steering events.
evidence: Based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: DNa02 predicts more transient changes in steering compared to DNa01.
source: Moreover, DNa02 predicts more transient changes in steering, as compared to DNa01.
evidence: Based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: At the onset of a steering bout, DNa02 is recruited earlier, and its firing rate fluctuations are more transient than those of DNa01.
source: At the onset of a steering bout, DNa02 is recruited earlier, and its firing rate fluctuations are more transient than those of DNa01.
evidence: Based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 play specialized roles in steering control.
source: All these results argue that these two DNs play specialized roles.
evidence: Inferred from the distinct functional profiles of DNa01 and DNa02.

claim: Both DNs can lengthen the stance phase of the ipsilateral back leg and/or decrease the step length in the ipsilateral legs, either of which would promote ipsiversive turning.
source: However, our optogenetic experiments suggest that both DNs can lengthen the stance phase of the ipsilateral back leg (Figure 8G), and/or decrease the step length in the ipsilateral legs (Figure 8H), either of which would promote ipsiversive turning.
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic inhibition experiments shown in Figure 8G and H.

claim: DNa02 receives stronger and more direct input from some steering circuits in the brain compared to DNa01.
source: This may be due to the fact that DNa02 receives stronger and more direct input from some steering circuits in the brain (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 based on connectome analysis.

claim: Yang et al., 2023 and Feng et al., 2024 confirmed that unilateral excitation of DNa02 produced ipsilateral body rotation.
source: Specifically, Yang et al., 2023 and Feng et al., 2024 tested the effect of unilateral excitation of DNa02 (using a different genetic strategy), and found that this produced ipsilateral body rotation, consistent with our results.
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2023 and Feng et al., 2024.

claim: Feng et al., 2024 confirmed that bilateral ablation of DNa02 significantly reduced the velocity of corrective turning maneuvers induced by errors in the head direction system.
source: Feng et al., 2024 also confirmed that bilateral ablation of DNa02 significantly reduced the velocity of corrective turning maneuvers induced by errors in the head direction system, and this supports our conclusion that DNa02 is recruited by the central complex for control of head direction.
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2024.

claim: Braun et al., 2024 reported that bilateral optogenetic activation of DNa02 or DNa01 can drive turning in either direction.
source: Meanwhile, Braun et al., 2024 reported that bilateral optogenetic activation of DNa02 or DNa01 can drive turning in either direction.
evidence: Supported by citation to Braun et al., 2024.

claim: Yang et al., 2023 found that perturbing DNa02 mainly affected ipsilateral leg movements.
source: Interestingly, Yang et al., 2023 found that perturbing DNa02 mainly affected ipsilateral leg movements, whereas (during voluntary turns) DNa02 activity was actually correlated with both ipsi- and contra legs, with opposite changes in the step cycle on the two sides of the body (Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2023.

claim: Brain connectome analyses explain the effect that DNa02 activity is correlated with both ipsi- and contra legs, with opposite changes in the step cycle on the two sides of the body.
source: Our brain connectome analyses in this study actually explain this effect. Specifically, we show that the brain inputs onto DNa02 are arranged so as to produce concurrent excitation of one copy and inhibition of the other copy, a see-saw arrangement that should generate opposite leg movement changes on the two sides of the body.
evidence: Inferred from connectome analysis.

claim: Yang et al., 2023 found that unilateral inhibition of DNa02 had no measurable effect on body rotation, but it significantly increased ipsilateral step length.
source: Yang et al., 2023 found that unilateral inhibition of DNa02 had no measurable effect on body rotation, but it significantly increased ipsilateral step length.
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2023.

claim: Bilateral DNa02 inhibition decreases step length bilaterally.
source: This is reminiscent of our finding that bilateral DNa02 inhibition decreases step length bilaterally (as does bilateral inhibition of DNa01).
evidence: Based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Bilateral inhibition of DNa01 decreases step length bilaterally.
source: This is reminiscent of our finding that bilateral DNa02 inhibition decreases step length bilaterally (as does bilateral inhibition of DNa01).
evidence: Based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Bilaterally optogenetically inhibiting DNa01 decreased the fly's forward velocity.
source: In this study, we found that bilaterally optogenetically inhibiting DNa01 decreased the fly's forward velocity.
evidence: Based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 are only weakly correlated with forward velocity during normal locomotion.
source: However, our electrophysiological results show that DNa01 and DNa02 are only weakly correlated with forward velocity during normal locomotion.
evidence: Based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: DNa01 and DNa02 are normally recruited by the brain for steering control.
source: In short, it seems that DNa01 and DNa02 are normally recruited by the brain for steering control, but bilateral perturbations can nonetheless produce forward velocity changes.
evidence: Inferred from the weak correlation with forward velocity during normal locomotion and the effects of bilateral perturbations.

claim: Many DNs actually influence steering during walking.
source: Finally, there is emerging evidence that many DNs actually influence steering during walking.
evidence: Based on emerging evidence from multiple studies.

claim: Optogenetically inhibiting DNa01 produced only small defects in steering.
source: We found that optogenetically inhibiting DNa01 produced only small defects in steering, and inhibiting DNa02 did not produce statistically significant effects on steering; these results make sense if DNa02 is just one of many steering DNs.
evidence: Based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Inhibiting DNa02 did not produce statistically significant effects on steering.
source: We found that optogenetically inhibiting DNa01 produced only small defects in steering, and inhibiting DNa02 did not produce statistically significant effects on steering; these results make sense if DNa02 is just one of many steering DNs.
evidence: Based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Several subsequent studies identified additional steering DNs, including DNg13, DNb05, and DNb06.
source: Indeed, while this study was in revision, several subsequent studies identified additional steering DNs, including DNg13, DNb05, and DNb06 (Yang et al., 2023), DNa11, DNae003, DNa03, and DNae014 (Feng et al., 2024), and DNb02 (Braun et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2024; Braun et al., 2024.

claim: Several subsequent studies identified additional steering DNs, including DNa11, DNae003, DNa03, and DNae014.
source: Indeed, while this study was in revision, several subsequent studies identified additional steering DNs, including DNg13, DNb05, and DNb06 (Yang et al., 2023), DNa11, DNae003, DNa03, and DNae014 (Feng et al., 2024), and DNb02 (Braun et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2024; Braun et al., 2024.

claim: Several subsequent studies identified DNb02 as an additional steering DN.
source: Indeed, while this study was in revision, several subsequent studies identified additional steering DNs, including DNg13, DNb05, and DNb06 (Yang et al., 2023), DNa11, DNae003, DNa03, and DNae014 (Feng et al., 2024), and DNb02 (Braun et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2024; Braun et al., 2024.

claim: Some DNs involved in steering control are organized hierarchically, with specific 'broadcaster' DNs subsequently recruiting other DNs with more specialized functions.
source: Several subsequent studies have also provided evidence that some DNs involved in steering control are organized hierarchically, with specific 'broadcaster' DNs subsequently recruiting other DNs with more specialized functions (Braun et al., 2024; Sapkal et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Braun et al., 2024; Sapkal et al., 2024.

claim: DNa02 is downstream from DNa03, a broadcaster DN that seems to promote decreases in forward speed as well as ipsiversive steering.
source: For example, DNa02 is downstream from DNa03, a broadcaster DN that seems to promote decreases in forward speed as well as ipsiversive steering (Feng et al., 2024; Westeinde et al., 2024); DNa02 is also downstream from DNp09, a broadcaster DN that can promote increases in forward speed as well as ipsiversive steering (Bidaye et al., 2020; Braun et al., 2024; Sapkal et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Feng et al., 2024; Westeinde et al., 2024.

claim: DNa02 is downstream from DNp09, a broadcaster DN that can promote increases in forward speed as well as ipsiversive steering.
source: For example, DNa02 is downstream from DNa03, a broadcaster DN that seems to promote decreases in forward speed as well as ipsiversive steering (Feng et al., 2024; Westeinde et al., 2024); DNa02 is also downstream from DNp09, a broadcaster DN that can promote increases in forward speed as well as ipsiversive steering (Bidaye et al., 2020; Braun et al., 2024; Sapkal et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bidaye et al., 2020; Braun et al., 2024; Sapkal et al., 2024.

claim: The DNs that target the wings and the legs are largely distinct populations.
source: The DNs that target the wings and the legs are largely distinct populations (Namiki et al., 2018), and the DNs currently implicated in steering during flight are distinct from those we have identified here (Ros et al., 2024; Schnell et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Namiki et al., 2018; Ros et al., 2024; Schnell et al., 2017.

claim: The DNs currently implicated in steering during flight are distinct from those identified in this study.
source: The DNs that target the wings and the legs are largely distinct populations (Namiki et al., 2018), and the DNs currently implicated in steering during flight are distinct from those we have identified here (Ros et al., 2024; Schnell et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ros et al., 2024; Schnell et al., 2017.

claim: DNa02 has indirect connectivity onto wing motor neurons, suggesting it contributes to steering during flight.
source: However, DNa02 does have indirect connectivity onto wing motor neurons, suggesting it contributes to steering during flight (Cheong et al., 2023).
evidence: Inferred from connectome analysis and supported by citation to Cheong et al., 2023.

claim: DNa03 activation can promote turning in flight, as well as turning during walking.
source: Moreover, a study subsequent to this work reported that DNa03 activation can promote turning in flight, as well as turning during walking (Feng et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2024.

claim: The GABAergic cell VES041 can suppress steering during flight.
source: Interestingly, the GABAergic cell VES041 can suppress steering during flight (Ros et al., 2024), and we predict that it has a similar role during walking, based on its connectivity upstream from DNa02.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ros et al., 2024.

claim: VES041 is predicted to have a similar role during walking, based on its connectivity upstream from DNa02.
source: Interestingly, the GABAergic cell VES041 can suppress steering during flight (Ros et al., 2024), and we predict that it has a similar role during walking, based on its connectivity upstream from DNa02.
evidence: Inferred from connectome analysis.

claim: Clear responses to lateralized sensory stimuli were observed in steering DNs even when the fly was not walking.
source: In this regard, it is notable that we observed clear responses to lateralized sensory stimuli in steering DNs even when the fly was not walking.
evidence: Based on experimental data.

claim: Drosophila DNs that evoke landing during flight are still responsive to visual stimuli when the fly is not flying.
source: Similarly, a recent study found that Drosophila DNs that evoke landing during flight are still responsive to visual stimuli when the fly is not flying (Ache et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ache et al., 2019.

claim: Residual DN responses can be thought of as a latent bias toward action, or a preparation for an action that never ultimately occurs.
source: We might think of these residual DN responses as a latent bias toward action, or a preparation for an action that never ultimately occurs (Kien, 1990).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of DN responses during immobility and supported by citation to Kien, 1990.

claim: Mammalian corticospinal neurons can be active in the absence of movement, either in the period preceding a movement or when a movement is being simply observed.
source: In this regard, it is relevant that mammalian corticospinal neurons can be active in the absence of movement, either in the period preceding a movement (Tanji and Evarts, 1976) or when a movement is being simply observed (Kraskov et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tanji and Evarts, 1976; Kraskov et al., 2014.

claim: Latent corticospinal signals may represent movement preparation, which may additionally involve neurons which are not actually active during movement.
source: These latent corticospinal signals may represent movement preparation, which may additionally involve neurons which are not actually active during movement (Churchland et al., 2010), and they may be responsible for driving latent activity in spinal neurons in the absence of movement (Prut and Fetz, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Churchland et al., 2010; Prut and Fetz, 1999.

claim: The discovery of latent motor activity in the Drosophila brain provides a potential starting point for future mechanistic investigations of brain dynamics during motor preparation.
source: The discovery of latent motor activity in the Drosophila brain provides a potential starting point for future mechanistic investigations of brain dynamics during motor preparation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of latent DN responses and the potential for future research.

claim: Behavioral state transitions may be organized, at least in part, via the network of cells presynaptic to DNs ('pre-DNs') in the lateral accessory lobe.
source: Behavioral state transitions may be organized, at least in part, via the network of cells presynaptic to DNs ('pre-DNs') in the lateral accessory lobe (Namiki and Kanzaki, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Namiki and Kanzaki, 2016.

claim: DNa03 and LAL010 both receive bilateral input from cell types known to exert high-level premotor control, namely PFL2 and VES041.
source: Our analyses highlight the anatomical features of several pre-DNs, most notably DNa03 and LAL010, which both receive bilateral input from cell types known to exert high-level premotor control, namely PFL2 (Westeinde et al., 2024) and VES041 (Ros et al., 2024).
evidence: Based on connectome analysis and supported by citations to Westeinde et al., 2024; Ros et al., 2024.

claim: LAL013 has recently been shown to play an important role in modulating steering.
source: Another pre-DN with similar connectivity (LAL013) has recently been shown to play an important role in modulating steering (Feng et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2024.

claim: Steering is driven by combinations of DNs with distinct functional roles, recruited by distinct parallel pathways in the brain, and targeting largely non-overlapping sets of cells in the ventral cord.
source: Our work shows that steering is driven by combinations of DNs with distinct functional roles, recruited by distinct parallel pathways in the brain, and targeting largely non-overlapping sets of cells in the ventral cord.
evidence: Summarizes findings from this study.

claim: Any walking or running organism faces the same basic physical constraints.
source: These results are relevant to vertebrates, because any walking or running organism faces the same basic physical constraints (Dickinson et al., 2000), and so it is likely that evolution has found a common set of solutions to these basic problems.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dickinson et al., 2000.

claim: It is likely that evolution has found a common set of solutions to the basic physical constraints of walking or running.
source: These results are relevant to vertebrates, because any walking or running organism faces the same basic physical constraints (Dickinson et al., 2000), and so it is likely that evolution has found a common set of solutions to these basic problems.
evidence: Inferred from the common physical constraints and supported by citation to Dickinson et al., 2000.

claim: Recent work has begun to identify the DNs that influence steering in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, recent work has begun to identify the DNs that influence steering (Cregg et al., 2020; Usseglio et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cregg et al., 2020; Usseglio et al., 2020.

claim: Vertebrate steering DNs should also be diverse and specialized.
source: Based on our results, we would predict that vertebrate steering DNs should also be diverse and specialized.
evidence: Inferred from the findings in Drosophila.

claim: Orienting behaviors are fundamental and ubiquitous indicators of an organism's perceptions and intentions.
source: In all species, orienting behaviors are fundamental and ubiquitous indicators of an organism's perceptions and intentions.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of animal behavior.

claim: Orienting behaviors provide a useful window into perception and cognition.
source: As such, they provide a useful window into perception and cognition.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of animal behavior.

claim: Once we fully understand the specializations of the DNs that control steering and orienting, we should be able to reframe the problem of controlling an organism's orientation as a more concrete problem of generating a specific pattern of DN dynamics.
source: Once we fully understand the specializations of the DNs that control steering and orienting, we should be able to reframe the problem of controlling an organism's orientation as a more concrete problem of generating a specific pattern of DN dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from the findings of this study and the potential for future research.

claim: This motor-centric perspective allows us to understand sensory and cognitive computations as solutions to specific problems of dynamical system control.
source: This motor-centric perspective then allows us to understand sensory and cognitive computations as solutions to specific problems of dynamical system control.
evidence: Inferred from the motor-centric perspective proposed in this study.
